terminal.description: The screen runs in the Browser panel and reloads every time you save. This shell opens in your workspace in case you want to look around.

tasks.title: Show the date and today's tram
tasks.description:
In `RideBoard`, take the date and the tram from `today` instead of typing them in:

- the `<h2>` shows `today.date`
- the paragraph with the class `tram` reads `No. ` and the tram's number, a comma, then the tram's name, like `No. 14, The Foundry Belle`

The check gives the board two days of its own and reads both lines.
nextSteps: Read "Curly braces open a window to JavaScript" in the lesson.
Open `src/today.js` and find the date, the tram's number and its name.
Replace the typed date in the `h2` with the value from `today`.
Do the same for the number and the name in the tram line.
hints: Everything on the board was typed in by hand. Each piece of it is somewhere in `today`.
Curly braces in JSX hold a JavaScript expression, and text can sit around them on the same line. The tram is an object inside `today`, so its fields are one dot further in.

The heading is `

{today.date}

`, and the tram line mixes text with `{today.tram.number}` and `{today.tram.name}`.

tasks.title: Show the ride times
tasks.description:
Two more lines come from `today`:

- the paragraph with the class `times` reads `First ride ` and `today.firstRide`, then `, last ride ` and `today.lastRide`
- the paragraph with the class `every` reads `A tram every 30 minutes` when there are two rides an hour. Work the minutes out from `today.ridesPerHour`: an hour divided by the rides in it.

The check gives the board days with other times and other numbers of rides an hour.
nextSteps: Find the two ride times in `today` and put them in the `times` line.
Work out on paper how many minutes apart three rides an hour are.
Write that sum inside the braces in the `every` line, using `today.ridesPerHour`.
If the board shows NaN, look at the spelling of the field.
hints: The times go in the same way as the date. The minutes are the new part: they are not in `today`, so they have to be worked out.
The braces take any expression that gives a value, a sum included. An hour has 60 minutes.
The every line is `A tram every {60 / today.ridesPerHour} minutes`.

tasks.title: Show the fares
tasks.description:
The paragraph with the class `fare` reads `Adult `, the adult fare, `, child `, then the child fare, like `Adult £3.50, child £1.75`.

- the adult fare is `today.farePence`
- a child pays half of it
- both are written with `formatPence` from `src/money.js`, which turns pence into text like `£3.50`

The check gives the board other fares and reads the line.
nextSteps: Read "Anything that gives a value" in the lesson.
Read `formatPence` in `src/money.js`: what it takes and what it gives back.
Call it for the adult fare inside the braces.
Call it again for the child fare, with half of the pence.
hints: `formatPence` is a function. Inside the braces it has to be called, like anywhere else in JavaScript.
Work out the child fare in pence first, then hand that number to `formatPence`. Halving the text it gives back does not work.
The line has the shape `Adult {formatPence(...)}, child {formatPence(... / 2)}`.

tasks.title: Show the photo of today's tram
tasks.description: The `` on the board still shows yesterday's tram. Give it values from `today`: - its `src` is the tram's `photo` - its `alt` is the tram's `name` The check gives the board other trams and reads both attributes of the image.
nextSteps: Read "Attributes take values too" in the lesson.
Find the photo and the name of the tram in `today`.
Give `src` and `alt` their values from `today`.
Save: the picture of tram 14 should appear on the board.
hints: An attribute in quotes is text that never changes.
An attribute can take a value from JavaScript the same way text can, with one difference in what goes around it.
Replace the quotes with curly braces: `src={today.tram.photo}`, and the same for `alt`.

tasks.title: Paint the livery strip
tasks.description:
Every tram is painted in its own colour, its livery, and the board has a strip for it: the `div` with the class `livery`. Set the strip's background to `today.tram.livery` with the `style` attribute.

The check gives the board trams of other colours and reads the background of the strip. A warning from React about a style name fails the task.
nextSteps: Read "Styles are objects" in the lesson.
Find the livery colour in `today`.
Give the strip a `style` whose background is that colour.
Look at the console in the Browser panel: it should show no warning.
hints: In JSX, `style` does not take a line of CSS.
It takes an object, and an object inside curly braces gives two pairs of braces. The CSS property is a key of that object.
`style={{ background: today.tram.livery }}` on the strip. `backgroundColor` works too.
